(p-4320) Sūrat al-Ḥajj

It was named so because it includes the basis of the obligation of the pilgrimage (ḥajj) and its principal aim among its pillars, which is the circumambulation (ṭawāf), since ihram is an intention, standing at ʿArafat is its preparation, the sa'y is its completion, and shaving (ḥalq) is the exit from it.

It also mentions its benefits (manāfiʿ), the glorification of its rites (shaʿāʾir), and other matters that point to its benefits and secrets. This was stated by al-Mahayimi.

It is related from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that it is Meccan except for three verses, "These are two adversaries..." up to the end of the three verses, for they were revealed in Medina. In other reports it is said that all of it is Medinan, as in al-Itqan. Its verses number seventy-eight.

(p-4321) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾

{ ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ } Exalted is He commands His servants to have taqwa (God-consciousness, piety), which is among the comprehensive words, in performing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden.

Al-Mahayimi said: That is, preserve His nurture over you by directing His blessings to the purposes for which He created them, lest you fall into ingratitude (kufr), which necessitates the reversal of His nurture upon you through retribution against you. End of quote.

That is, the mention of the title of Lordship (rubūbiyyah), which indicates ownership and nurture, together with the addition to the pronoun of the addressees, serves to reinforce the command and to emphasize the obligation of complying with it, both through encouragement and warning. That is: beware of the punishment of the Owner of your affairs and your Nurturer. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾, is a reason for the requirement of the command, by mentioning some of its terrible punishments. For the awareness of its greatness and terror, and the horror of what precedes it and its beginnings of conditions and terrors, from which there is no refuge except by clothing oneself in the garment of taqwa, necessarily requires greater care in adhering to it and persisting in it. The "convulsion" (zalzalah) is a violent shaking and a vehement disturbance, by repetition, to the extent that it removes things from their places and displaces them from their positions. Its attribution to "the Hour" is an attribution of the verbal noun to its agent metaphorically, as if it were the one that shakes; or to its time, namely the convulsion mentioned in His saying, ﴿When the earth is shaken with its convulsion﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1]. The expression of it as "a thing" (shayʾ) indicates that minds fall short of grasping its reality, and that expression cannot encompass it except in a vague manner. This was stated by Abu al-Suʿud.

Its greatness has been described in many surahs and verses, such as Surat al-Takwir, Surat al-Infitar (p-4322) Surat al-Inshiqaq, Surat al-Zalzalah, and others. Some of its dreadful terror has been indicated by His saying, glorified is He:

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 22, verse 2:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed, and every pregnant woman will drop her load, and you will see people as drunk, though they are not drunk, but the punishment of God is severe.﴾

{ ﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾ } That is: from nursing it. Or: from that which she nursed, namely the infant. { ﴿and every pregnant woman will drop her load﴾ } That is: what is in her womb, before its completion. { ﴿and you will see people as drunk﴾ } That is: as though they were drunk. { ﴿though they are not drunk﴾ } That is: in reality. { ﴿but the punishment of God is severe﴾ } That is: but what overwhelmed them of the fear of God's punishment is what took away their minds, dispelled their discernment, and reduced them to a state resembling that of one whose intoxication has taken away his reason and discernment. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

A subtle point:

Al-Nasir said in (al-Intisaf): The scholars say that among the indicators of metaphor is that its opposite is true. As when you say, "Zayd is a donkey," describing him with dullness, and then it is correct to say, "He is not a donkey," negating the literal reality. So it is with the verse. After the metaphorical drunkenness is affirmed, the literal is negated with the most emphatic negation, reinforced by the particle bi (ب). The secret in its confirmation is to draw attention to the fact that this drunkenness which they are in at that state is not like anything familiar; rather it is a matter they had not known before its like. The adversative "but" in His saying, { ﴿but the punishment of God is severe﴾ }, refers back to His saying { ﴿and they are not drunk﴾ }, as though it were a reason for affirming the metaphorical drunkenness. It is as if it were said: If they are not drunk from wine, which is the familiar drunkenness, then what is this strange drunkenness and what is its cause? So He said: its cause is the severity of God's punishment, exalted is He. End.

(p-4323) Then the state of those who deny the Hour is indicated by His saying, exalted is He:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[3] ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge, and follows every rebellious devil.﴾

{﴿And among the people is one who disputes about Allah without knowledge﴾} That is: he argues concerning the matter of Allah, Exalted is He, without knowledge. So he claims that He is unable to bring to life one who has decayed and become dust, and other such falsehoods. {﴿And follows﴾} That is, in his disputing, {﴿every rebellious devil﴾} That is: every insolent, defiant one, such as the leaders of disbelief who turn people away from the truth. Then he points to another attribute of this followed devil, by His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[4] ﴿It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾

{﴿It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾} That is: it has been decreed against the Devil that he will lead astray whoever takes him as a guardian by making him a friend and following him, and he will not guide him to the truth, but will drive him toward the punishment of Hell, the kindled fire. His driving him toward it is by calling him to obey him and to disobey the Most Merciful.

Note:

It was said: the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was a disputatious man.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is general in its application to everyone who engages in disputation about what is permissible for God and what is not permissible, regarding His attributes and actions, without returning to knowledge and without biting upon it with a decisive molar tooth. There is in it no following of proof and no yielding to fairness, so he stumbles blindly like one who has lost his way in the dark, not distinguishing between truth and falsehood. End of quotation.

Then Almighty God presented the conclusive proof against what they dispute about, saying:

Discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[5] ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop (nutfah), then from a clinging clot (alaqah), then from a lump of flesh (mudghah), formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs what We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as a child, then [We let you reach] your maturity (ashudd), and among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful kind of pair.﴾

﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾ meaning: about its possibility and that it is within His power, Exalted is He, or about its occurrence. ﴿Then indeed We created you from dust﴾ meaning: We created your first father, or your first constituent, which is the seminal fluid (maniyy), from dust, since it was created from nourishment derived from it. The most that can be said about the matter of resurrection is that you were created from dust. ﴿Then from a drop﴾ meaning: produced from earthly nourishment. ﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾ meaning: a piece of congealed blood. ﴿Then from a lump of flesh﴾ meaning: a piece of flesh the size of what can be chewed. ﴿Formed and unformed﴾ meaning: shaped and unshaped. The purpose is to detail the state of the lump of flesh: at first it was a piece in which no part of the limbs had appeared, and then they appeared gradually, little by little. ﴿That We may make clear to you﴾ meaning: through this gradual process, Our power and Our wisdom, and that what preceded change, corruption and existence once, existed before it, and that He who is able to alter it and shape it first is able to do so a second time. ﴿And We settle in the wombs what We will for a specified term﴾, which is the time of delivery.

Abu al-Su'ud said: this is a resumptive statement brought to explain their condition after the completion of their creation. The non-inclusion of this and what is conjoined to it within the chain of creation that is causally linked to "making clear," although these are among its completions and among the beginnings of making clear too, is because the indication of the first (the creation) of the perfection of His power, Exalted is He, over all things capable of being done, of which the resurrection under discussion is one, is more evident and manifest. That is: and We settle in the wombs after that what We will to settle in them for a specified term.

﴿Then We bring you out as a child, then [We let you reach] your maturity (ashudd)﴾ meaning: the perfection of your strength and your intellect. Abu al-Su'ud said: it is a cause for "We bring you out," conjoined to another cause parallel to it, as if it were said: then We bring you out so that you grow gradually, then so that you attain your perfection in strength and discernment. ﴿And among you is one who is taken in death﴾ meaning: after reaching maturity or before it. ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾, which is senility and dotage. Al-ardhal means the worst: ﴿so that he knows nothing after having known﴾ meaning: after much knowledge, nothing of things, or nothing of knowledge, as an exaggeration of the diminution of his knowledge and the reversal of his condition. The lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah).

Al-Baydawi said: the verse, namely ﴿Then We bring you out﴾ etc., is a second argument for the possibility of resurrection, from the various matters and contrary states that befall a person across his ages. For whoever is able to do that is able to do its like.

Then Almighty God pointed to another proof for the soundness of resurrection, saying: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾ meaning: dead and dry. ﴿But when We send down water upon it﴾ meaning: rain. ﴿It stirs﴾ meaning: it moves with vegetation. ﴿Swells﴾ meaning: it swells and rises, because the water penetrates into it and its vegetation rises above it. ﴿And grows every kind of pair﴾ meaning: every species, ﴿beautiful﴾ meaning: goodly and delightful, pleasing its beholder. This is the third proof, and because of its evidence and because it is witnessed and observed, Almighty God repeats it in His Noble Book.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6–7] ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is capable of all things﴾ ﴿and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and that Allah will raise those who are in the graves﴾ [al-Hajj: 7].

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ means: that which was mentioned, of the creation of man in various stages, His disposing of him in differing conditions, and the giving of life to the earth after its death, occurs because Allah is the Truth [p. 4326] alone in His essence, His attributes and His actions, the one who establishes the reality of everything else. Thus, other things are among the effects of His divinity and His essential affairs alone. Whatever is other than Him is falsehood, far removed, and has no power over any of that. ﴿And that He gives life to the dead﴾ means: He is able to bring them to life, since He brought the drop of semen and the dead earth to life. ﴿And that He is capable of all things﴾: for the power by which He made these wondrous things is not restrained from anything. ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Hajj: 7] means: because wisdom requires it. Its rational proofs are so clear that there is no ground for anyone to doubt its coming. ﴿And that Allah will raise those who are in the graves﴾ [al-Hajj: 7] means: the dead, being brought back to life for the place of reckoning.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 22, verses 8–10:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[8–10] ﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾ ﴿turning aside, to mislead from the way of Allah. For him in this world is disgrace, and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] ﴿That is for what your hands have put forth, and that Allah is not ever unjust to His servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10].

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾ That is: he argues concerning the affair of Allah, Exalted is He, without holding to necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī, knowledge that is self-evident and does not require proof), nor to valid inference and sound reflection (naẓar) that leads to knowledge, nor to revelation that makes the truth manifest. Rather, he relies only on mere opinion and whim. This verse refers to the callers to misguidance from the leaders of disbelief, who are followers of others (muqallidīn), with the lam pronounced with a fatḥa (muqallidīn, i.e., those who are led). Just as the verse before it refers to the misguided ignorant ones who are followers, with the lam pronounced with a kasra (muqallidīn, i.e., those who follow). So there is no repetition. Or the two verses refer to the misleading callers, and the differing descriptions of them are taken into account, so there is no repetition either.

In al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari's work), it is said: "The first (interpretation) is more evident and more fitting to the context." Abu Muslim also chose this, as al-Razi transmitted from him. Then he said: "If it is said, how can what you have said be correct, since the follower (muqallid) is not one who argues? We say: He may argue in order to justify his imitation, and he may present an apparent doubt when he is able to do so, even though his fundamental basis is imitation."

(p-4327) His saying: ﴿turning aside﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of (yujādilu, "argues"). That is: he turns his side away in aversion and arrogance from the truth when he is called to it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Turning the side (thaniyu al-ʿiṭf) is an expression for pride and conceit, like turning the cheek away (taṣʿīr al-khadd) and twisting the neck." His saying: ﴿to mislead from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] means: to turn away from His religion and His law. It is connected to (yujādilu) as its cause. ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] means: humiliation and abasement, as befell him on the day of Badr of ignominy and defeat. ﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Hajj: 9] means: the blazing Fire. ﴿That is for what your hands have put forth﴾ [al-Hajj: 10] is by way of iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person), or by implying a saying: it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: that disgrace and punishment is because of what you committed of disbelief, misguidance, and misleading others. Its attribution to his hands is because acquiring (iktisāb) is ordinarily done by the hands. ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to His servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10] means: rather, He is the Just in punishing the wicked and rewarding the righteous.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted Saying:

[11] ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge. If good befalls him, he is reassured by it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost the world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾

﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge﴾ This begins the description of the wavering people (al-mudhabdhabun), following the explanation of the state of the emigrants. That is: among them is one who worships Him, exalted is He, on the fringe of the religion, not at its center and in its heart. This is a parable for their being in unease and turmoil in their religion, not in tranquility and composure, like one who inclines to the edge of the army: if he senses victory and booty, he stays; otherwise he flees. ﴿If good befalls him﴾, that is, worldly good of health and abundance, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾, that is, he remains outwardly upon what he was upon. ﴿But if a trial befalls him﴾, that is, whatever tests him of adversity that descends upon him, ﴿he turns back on his face﴾, that is, he returns to what he was upon of disbelief. ﴿He has lost﴾, that is, by this turning back, ﴿the world﴾ [al-A'la: 16] ﴿and the Hereafter﴾ [al-A'la: 17], that is, he has squandered both by the loss of his protection and the nullification of his deeds through apostasy. ﴿That is the manifest loss﴾, that is, the clear loss that is not hidden from one who has insight.

(p-4328) Notice:

Ibn Jarir said: By His saying, exalted is His remembrance, ﴿And among the people﴾ etc., He means some Bedouin Arabs who used to come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as emigrants from their desert dwellings. If they attained ease, from livelihood after the emigration and entering into Islam, they remained upon Islam; otherwise they turned back upon their heels. The people of interpretation said in accordance with what we have said, and he traced it through several chains.

This is among the things that support that the surah is Medinan, as a group has said, and this has preceded. And His Exalted Saying:

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[12] ﴿He calls, besides Allah, upon that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-reaching error.﴾

﴿He calls, besides Allah, upon that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ means: this is a established state (ḥāl thābita) from the subject of (inqalaba) [he turned back on his heels], while the first (khasira) [he lost] ... and for this reason it was read (khāsir) [a losing one], i.e., he apostatized from the religion of Allah, calling upon other than Him gods that cannot harm him if he does not worship them in this world, nor benefit him in the Hereafter if he worships them. Abu al-Su'ud said: (yad'u) is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) explaining the magnitude of the loss: ﴿That is the far-reaching error﴾, i.e., far from the truth and guidance. And the words of Allah, the Exalted:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[13] ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-straying error. He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Wretched is the protector, and wretched the companion.﴾

﴿He calls upon﴾ means: this one who turns back on his face when a trial befalls him. ﴿One whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ means: an idol or a statue, whose harm, in this world through humiliation and disgrace and in the Hereafter through punishment, comes more swiftly to him than the benefit he expects from worshipping it, namely shafa'ah (intercession) and tawassul (seeking a means of access) to Allah, may He be exalted. The lam is then superfluous in the object, which is (man), as it is superfluous in His words ﴿It may be that some of what you seek to hasten has drawn close to you﴾ [al-Naml: 72], according to one view. It has been reported that Ibn Mas'ud used to recite it as { yad'u man darrahu } without the lam, and this supports the view that it is superfluous. (darrahu) is the subject (mubtada'), and (aqrabu) is its predicate. There are many other views on this verse, and this is the most apparent of them. The attribution of harm to it here is with regard to its being worshipped, whereas its negation earlier is with regard to its own essence. The verse functions as a correction or a turning away from what precedes it, affirming a certain harm that will befall its worshipper, as a way of foolishing and declaring ignorant the belief of the worshipper that he will obtain benefit from it when he seeks its intercession. The use of the comparative form, although it contains no benefit at all, serves to intensify the condemnation of its state and to go to the utmost in censuring it. ﴿Wretched is the protector﴾, that is, the helper of him; ﴿and wretched the companion﴾, that is, the one who accompanies him.

Having explained the evil state of the disbelievers, both the open ones and the wavering ones, He followed it with the perfect goodness of the state of the believers, by His words, may He be exalted:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[14] ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾ That is: of the acts that are founded upon wisdom, among which is the rewarding of those who obey Him and the punishing of those who disobey Him.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[15] ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will never give him victory in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky and then cut it off, and see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him.﴾

﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will never give him victory in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾ (p-4330) means: with a rope to what is above it. ﴿Then let him cut it off﴾ means: let him choke himself. ﴿Then let him look: will his scheming remove that which enrages him﴾ means: his rage. The meaning is: whoever is slow to see Allah's victory and seeks it hastily, let him kill himself, because it has an appointed time in which it alone will occur. The verse concerns a group of Muslims who were slow to see Allah's victory, due to their haste, their intense rage, and their fury toward the polytheists. It is also permissible that it concerns a group of polytheists, with the pronoun in "yansuruhu" (he gives him victory) referring to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning is: whoever among them thinks that Allah will not give victory to His Prophet, let him choke and destroy himself; then let him look into himself: will his scheme of harm and opposition remove what enrages him of the victory? No. Indeed Allah is the helper of His Messenger without doubt. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We surely help Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir: 51].

**The interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:**

[18] ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the moving creatures, and many of mankind? But many deserve the punishment. And whoever Allah humiliates, for him there is no honorer. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.﴾

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the moving creatures, and many of mankind﴾ is an explanation of His greatness, exalted is He, and of His being singular in His divinity (ulūhiyyah) and His lordship (rubūbiyyah), through the submission of these great realms to Him and their running in accordance with His command and His governance. Thus, the prostration (sujūd) in them is used figuratively (musta'ār) from its familiar meaning, because things comply with Him, exalted is He, in what He brings about in them of His acts, which He causes to run upon them from His management and subjection of them. The point of resemblance is attainment in accordance with the will, without refusal from them, in both cases.

His saying, ﴿and many of mankind﴾, is either conjoined to what precedes it, if it is permissible to use a homonymous word (lafẓ mushtarak) in both of its meanings together, so that prostration in inanimate things is submission and in rational beings is worship; or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted; or it is the agent (fā'il) of an omitted verb, if that is not permissible.

His exalted saying: ﴿But many deserve the punishment﴾ means: from among mankind, by their disbelief and their defiance. ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates﴾ means: by Him having written misery for him, according to what He knew of the turning of his choice toward evil. ﴿For him there is no honorer﴾ means: no one who honors him with happiness. ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[19] ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. But those who disbelieve, for them will be cut garments of fire; poured over their heads will be scalding water.﴾

﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ means the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, which is divided into the five groups explained in the previous verse. The word "khasm" (adversary) is originally a verbal noun (masdar), so it is usually used in the singular and indefinite form, and the singular masculine and other forms are alike in it. The meaning of ﴿they dispute concerning their Lord﴾ is: concerning their religion and their worship. The "ikhtisam" (disputing) includes both the actual dialogue that occurred at times between the people of the mentioned religions, and the dispute in meaning. For the belief of each of the two groups in the truth of what it holds, the falsehood of what its opponent holds, and the building of its sayings and actions upon that belief, is a dispute with the other group, even if dialogue and contention do not take place between them. Then He indicated the settling of their mentioned dispute, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 17], with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿But those who disbelieve﴾, meaning "were measured out" (qudirat): ﴿for them will be cut garments of fire; poured over their heads will be scalding water﴾, meaning the hot water.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[25] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque, which We made for the people, equal for the resident therein and the visitor, and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing - We will make him taste a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque﴾, i.e., Makkah. ﴿Which We made for the people, equal for the resident therein﴾, i.e., the one who stays there, ﴿and the visitor﴾, i.e., the one who comes and goes. ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation﴾, i.e., inclination away from the right course (ilhad, deviation). ﴿By wrongdoing﴾, i.e., without right. ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾, i.e., as a recompense for violating its sanctity. Deviation (ilhad) includes associating partners with Allah, preventing people from building up (i'mar) it, and committing sins. The verse indicates that whoever is in it is obliged to restrain himself and to follow the path of rectitude and justice in everything he intends and purposes. Some of the early generations (al-salaf) held that an evil deed committed in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) is greater than in other places, that it is multiplied there, and that if one intends it there, he is held accountable for it. The object of (yurid) is either omitted, i.e., "yurid shay'an" (intends something) or "muradan ma" (some purpose), and the ba' is for accompaniment (mulabasah). Or it is redundant, and (ilhadan) is its object. Or the ba' is for transitivity, by implying the meaning of (yaltabis, to be involved in). And (bi-zulmin) is a synonymous circumstantial clause (hal). Or it is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it, by repeating the preposition. Or it is a complement to it, i.e., deviating because of wrongdoing. In every case, it emphasizes what precedes it. From His saying ﴿We will make him taste﴾ and so on, the predicate of inna is derived, and it is implied after His saying ﴿and the visitor﴾, indicated by the end of the verse, as Abu Hayyan approved in (al-Bahr al-Muhit). (p-٤٣٣٤) Then Exalted is He pointed to the rebuke and censure of those who worshipped other than Him and associated partners with Him in this blessed place, which was founded from the first day upon the monotheism of Allah and the worship of Him alone, without partner, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[26] ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House, [saying]: "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate."﴾

﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾, i.e., remember when We designated it for him and made it for him a *mubā'ah* (a dwelling and a place of return), that is, a residence and a point of return for his worship of Him alone, exalted is He. The *an* (that) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that do not associate anything with Me﴾ is explanatory (*mufassirah*) of ﴿settled﴾, insofar as it contains the meaning of "We made [it] a place of worship (*ta'abbadnā*), because settling is for worship." That is: We did that so that you would not associate anything with Me. ﴿And purify My House﴾, i.e., from the idols, the images, and the impurities; ﴿for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate﴾, i.e., for those who circle it, stand in it, and pray. Or the intended meaning of "those who stand" and what follows is "those who pray" (*al-muṣallīn*), and He expressed prayer by its pillars (*arkān*), to indicate that each one of them independently necessitates that [purification], so how much more so when they are gathered together?

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[27–28] ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾ ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle. So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor﴾ [al-Hajj: 28].

﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj﴾ means: call out to them concerning it. Al-Zamakhshari said: The proclamation of the Hajj is that one says: "Perform Hajj," or "Upon you is the Hajj." ﴿They will come to you on foot﴾ means: walking, the plural of (rajil) [pedestrian]. ﴿And on every lean camel﴾ (p-4335) means: riding, upon every camel made lean, whose emaciation was caused by the distance of the journey that wore it out. The departure from "riding" to the more concise form serves to indicate the great number of those coming from distant places. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿they will come﴾ (yatūna) is a description of ﴿every lean camel﴾, because it carries the sense of a plural. It has also been read as a description of the men and the riders. Or it is a resumption (istinaf), in which case the pronoun refers to the people. ﴿From every deep mountain pass﴾ means: from a wide, distant path. ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ [al-Hajj: 28] means: that they may attend benefits for themselves, both religious and worldly. ﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle﴾ [al-Hajj: 28] means: over what He has made them possess of them and subjected them to them, so that they may make them offerings (hady) and sacrifices (dahaya). Al-Zamakhshari said: He alluded to slaughtering and sacrificing by mentioning the name of Allah, because the people of Islam do not cease from mentioning His name when they slaughter or sacrifice. In this there is an indication that the primary purpose in what is offered seeking nearness to Allah is that His name be mentioned, and that the polytheists be opposed in this, for they used to slaughter them for idols and images (nusub and awthan). Al-Qaffal said: It is as though the one who draws near by them, and by shedding their blood, is pictured in the form of one who ransoms himself with something equivalent. So it is as though he gives that sheep in place of his own life, seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, and acknowledging that his shortcoming nearly deserved his life. The known days are the days of the ten [nights]; or the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and three days, or two days after it; or the day of Arafah, the day of sacrifice, and a day after it. These are the sayings of the imams.

Ibn Kathir said: The second and third views are reinforced by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle﴾ [al-Hajj: 28], meaning: mentioning Allah at the time of their slaughter. End of quotation.

I say: It is not far-fetched that ʿalā (over) is causal (taʿlīliyyah), and the meaning is: that they may mention the name of Allah alone on those days, with His praise, thanks and glorification, on account of what He has provided for them of those beasts. For He alone is the Provider of them and the One who bestows them upon them as a favour. Had He willed, He would have forbidden them to them and made them wild, unruly beasts. He has bestowed this favour upon them in more than one place in His Noble Revelation, such as His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are their owners?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71] ﴿And We have subjected them to them, so from them is their riding and from them they eat﴾ [Ya-Sin: 72].

(p-4336) The secret in singling out this blessing and reminding of it, rather than others of His blessings and bounties, is that by them is the life of the Arabs and the sustenance of their livelihood, for from them come their food, drink, clothing, furnishings, tents, mounts and adornment. Had it not been for His, Exalted is He, favour upon them in subjecting them to them, no affair of theirs would have stood. For their land is not one of crops, and they are not people of renowned craft, nor is their peninsula civilized and urbane. Those who are in this state are most fitting to mention the One who bestows on them what sustains them, to thank Him and to recognize His right: by worshipping Him alone and exalting His sacred things and rites. Thus reflection upon them in this regard necessitates humbleness before their Provider, submission to Him and fear of Him. The parallel of the verse, as it appears to us, is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ [Quraysh: 3] ﴿Who fed them after hunger and secured them from fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4]. This is the first point. Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 22, verse 29–31:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[29–31] ﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness, fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.﴾ ﴿That is so. And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him with his Lord. And the cattle have been made lawful to you, except what is recited to you. So avoid the abomination of idols, and avoid the word of falsehood,﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] ﴿being people of pure faith (hunafa') to Allah, not associating anything with Him. And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind threw him into a remote place.﴾ [al-Hajj: 31].

﴿Then﴾, i.e., after the slaughter: ﴿let them end their state of unkemptness (tafath)﴾, i.e., let them remove the dirt of the state of ihram by shaving or trimming (the hair), cutting the nails, and wearing (ordinary) clothes. ﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾, i.e., what they have vowed of acts of righteousness during their pilgrimage. ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾, i.e., the circumambulation of ifada (ziyarah), which is one of the pillars of the Hajj, and by which the complete release from ihram is achieved. Al-'Atiq means "the ancient" (al-qadim), because it is the first house set up for mankind; or it means "the one freed from the domination of tyrants."

﴿That﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the matter is that. This and similar demonstratives are used to separate two statements, or two aspects of one statement.

Al-Shihab said: The well-known usage for separation is "hadha," as in His saying: ﴿This, and indeed for the transgressors is the worst of abodes.﴾ [Sad: 55] (p-4338) The choice of "dhalika" here is to indicate the greatness of the matter and the loftiness of its station. It is a form of abrupt transition (iqtidab) close to the transitional device (takhallus), because what follows fits what precedes, as here: ﴿And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], i.e., His rulings, or the Sacred Precinct and the rites connected with the Hajj. "Hurumat" is the plural of "hurmah," which is that which must not be violated but is to be respected by the Law. ﴿It is better for him with his Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], i.e., in reward. "Khayr" is an elative noun whose complement has been omitted, i.e., better than others; or it is not meant as a comparative, and so it needs no supposed complement, as al-Shihab said. The second view is the more apparent, because it is the style of revelation in a context where no comparison is evident. Its choice, despite this, is for the delicacy of its wording and its combination of beauty and awe. ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful to you, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], i.e., the verse of its prohibition, which is His saying in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The meaning is: Allah has made all cattle lawful to you, except what He has excepted in His Book. So observe His limits. Beware of prohibiting anything of what has been made lawful for you, like the idolaters' prohibition of the bahirah and sa'ibah and other things, or of making lawful what Allah has forbidden, like their permitting the eating of the mawquudhah and carrion and other things. This was conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] is a consequence of what preceded regarding the honoring of His sacred rites, for abandoning association and avoiding idols is among the greatest observances of His limits. "Min" here is explicative (bayaniyyah), i.e., avoid the abomination which is the idols, just as impurities are avoided. This is the utmost emphasis in forbidding their veneration and in warning against their worship. Al-Zamakhshari said: He called idols "rijs" (abomination), and likewise wine, gambling, and the divining arrows, by way of comparison. He made the reason for avoiding it that it is "rijs," and "rijs" is to be avoided. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And avoid the word of falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] is a generalization after a specification, for the worship of idols is the foremost of falsehood. It is as if, when He urged the honoring of the sacred rites, He followed this with it, as a refutation of what the unbelievers had been upon regarding the prohibition of the bahair and sawa'ib, and the glorifying of idols, and the fabrication against Allah that He had ruled thus, (p-4339) and as an announcement that the Oneness of Allah, the negation of partners from Him, and truthfulness of speech, are the greatest of sacred things and the first in precedence.

﴿Being people of pure faith (hunafa') to Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., sincerely devoted to Him in religion, turning away from falsehood toward truth. ﴿Not associating anything with Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., anything whatsoever. Then He struck a parable for the polytheist in his misguidance, his ruin, and his distance from guidance, saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., he fell from it, and the birds tore him apart in the air. ﴿Or the wind throws him﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., carries him away, ﴿into a remote place﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., a distant place, destructive to whoever falls into it. "Aw" here is for choice or for classification. Al-Zamakhshari said: In this simile it is possible that it is either a compound or a divided comparison. If it is a compound comparison, it is as if he said: whoever associates others with Allah has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is no end, by depicting his state as the state of one who fell from the sky, was snatched by birds, and was scattered into pieces in their crops, or the wind swept him until it dropped him in some distant abyss. If it is a divided comparison, he likened faith in its loftiness to the sky, the one who abandoned faith and associated others with Allah to the one who fell from the sky, the desires that scatter his thoughts to the snatching birds, and Satan who casts him into the valley of error to the wind that drops what it has swept into some destructive chasm. Al-Nasir commented on this: As for the assumption that it is divided, the explanation of likening the polytheist to one who falls from the sky requires pointing out one of two matters: either the association meant is apostasy, for then he is like one who rose to the sky by his faith and then descended by his apostasy; or the association is original, in which case it counts his capacity for faith and for rising through it, then his deliberate turning away from it, as like one who rose to the sky and then descended, as He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut, who bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. He counted them as having been brought out of the light, though they never entered it, but they were capable of it. In his explanation, there is a likening of the scattered thoughts of the unbeliever to the snatching birds, and in the likening of Satan's casting down to the wind carrying one into a remote place, there is scrutiny, because both matters were mentioned in the context of dividing the state of the unbeliever into two parts. If the first is made an example of the divergence of desires and thoughts, and the second an example of Satan's incitement, then he has made them one thing, because the scattering of thoughts and the divergence of desires are attributed to Satan's incitement, so the intended division is not realized. What appears in the explanation of the two likenesses is other than that. We say: when the state of disbelief was divided into two parts with no more beyond them, the first of them is the wavering one, persisting in doubt and not resolving upon a single error. This kind of polytheist is likened to one whom the birds have snatched and scattered, for no bird seizes a piece of him without another snatching it from it, and that is the state of the wavering one: no fancy appears to him without his following it and descending from what he was upon. The second is a polytheist resolved upon a false belief, who, even if sawn with a saw, would not yield or turn back; there is no way to make him doubt, and no hope of moving him from what he is upon, for he rejoices and is delighted in his error.

This one is likened, in his persistence in his disbelief, to the settling of one whom the wind has thrown into a low valley where he settles. The likeness to settling in the remote valley, which is the furthest of abysses from the sky, is evident. He described his error as distant in His saying: ﴿Those are in distant error﴾ [Ibrahim: 3] and ﴿They have certainly strayed far away﴾ [al-Nisa': 167], i.e., they resolved upon their error, so their return to the truth became remote. This is the realization of the two divisions, and Allah knows best. End of his words.

It is not hidden that in the noble text there is room for this, though there is no decisive proof for it. Yes, it is a marvelous deduction and a subtle extraction. May Allah have mercy on its copyist.

Ibn Kathir said: Allah, exalted is He, has struck for the polytheists another parable in Surat al-An'am, which is His saying: ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah what neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have led astray in the earth, bewildered, having companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us." Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 71], and so on.

﴿Then﴾, i.e., after the slaughter: ﴿let them end their state of unkemptness (tafath)﴾, i.e., let them remove the dirt of the state of ihram by shaving or trimming (the hair), cutting the nails, and wearing (ordinary) clothes. ﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾, i.e., what they have vowed of acts of righteousness during their pilgrimage. ﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾, i.e., the circumambulation of ifada (ziyarah), which is one of the pillars of the Hajj, and by which the complete release from ihram is achieved. Al-'Atiq means "the ancient" (al-qadim), because it is the first house set up for mankind; or it means "the one freed from the domination of tyrants."

﴿That﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the matter is that. This and similar demonstratives are used to separate two statements, or two aspects of one statement.

Al-Shihab said: The well-known usage for separation is "hadha," as in His saying: ﴿This, and indeed for the transgressors is the worst of abodes.﴾ [Sad: 55] (p-4338) The choice of "dhalika" here is to indicate the greatness of the matter and the loftiness of its station. It is a form of abrupt transition (iqtidab) close to the transitional device (takhallus), because what follows fits what precedes, as here: ﴿And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], i.e., His rulings, or the Sacred Precinct and the rites connected with the Hajj. "Hurumat" is the plural of "hurmah," which is that which must not be violated but is to be respected by the Law. ﴿It is better for him with his Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], i.e., in reward. "Khayr" is an elative noun whose complement has been omitted, i.e., better than others; or it is not meant as a comparative, and so it needs no supposed complement, as al-Shihab said. The second view is the more apparent, because it is the style of revelation in a context where no comparison is evident. Its choice, despite this, is for the delicacy of its wording and its combination of beauty and awe. ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful to you, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], i.e., the verse of its prohibition, which is His saying in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The meaning is: Allah has made all cattle lawful to you, except what He has excepted in His Book. So observe His limits. Beware of prohibiting anything of what has been made lawful for you, like the idolaters' prohibition of the bahirah and sa'ibah and other things, or of making lawful what Allah has forbidden, like their permitting the eating of the mawquudhah and carrion and other things. This was conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.

﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] is a consequence of what preceded regarding the honoring of His sacred rites, for abandoning association and avoiding idols is among the greatest observances of His limits. "Min" here is explicative (bayaniyyah), i.e., avoid the abomination which is the idols, just as impurities are avoided. This is the utmost emphasis in forbidding their veneration and in warning against their worship. Al-Zamakhshari said: He called idols "rijs" (abomination), and likewise wine, gambling, and the divining arrows, by way of comparison. He means: just as you recoil from filth by your natures and avoid it, so you must recoil from these things with the same recoiling. He drew attention to this meaning with His saying: ﴿An abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]. He made the reason for avoiding it that it is "rijs," and "rijs" is to be avoided. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And avoid the word of falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] is a generalization after a specification, for the worship of idols is the foremost of falsehood. It is as if, when He urged the honoring of the sacred rites, He followed this with it, as a refutation of what the unbelievers had been upon regarding the prohibition of the bahair and sawa'ib, and the glorifying of idols, and the fabrication against Allah that He had ruled thus, (p-4339) and as an announcement that the Oneness of Allah, the negation of partners from Him, and truthfulness of speech, are the greatest of sacred things and the first in precedence.

﴿Being people of pure faith (hunafa') to Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., sincerely devoted to Him in religion, turning away from falsehood toward truth. ﴿Not associating anything with Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., anything whatsoever. Then He struck a parable for the polytheist in his misguidance, his ruin, and his distance from guidance, saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., he fell from it, and the birds tore him apart in the air. ﴿Or the wind throws him﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., carries him away, ﴿into a remote place﴾ [al-Hajj: 31], i.e., a distant place, destructive to whoever falls into it. "Aw" here is for choice or for classification. Al-Zamakhshari said: In this simile it is possible that it is either a compound or a divided comparison. If it is a compound comparison, it is as if he said: whoever associates others with Allah has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is no end, by depicting his state as the state of one who fell from the sky, was snatched by birds, and was scattered into pieces in their crops, or the wind swept him until it dropped him in some distant abyss. If it is a divided comparison, he likened faith in its loftiness to the sky, the one who abandoned faith and associated others with Allah to the one who fell from the sky, the desires that scatter his thoughts to the snatching birds, and Satan who casts him into the valley of error to the wind that drops what it has swept into some destructive chasm. Al-Nasir commented on this: As for the assumption that it is divided, the explanation of likening the polytheist to one who falls from the sky requires pointing out one of two matters: either the association meant is apostasy, for then he is like one who rose to the sky by his faith and then descended by his apostasy; or the association is original, in which case it counts his capacity for faith and for rising through it, then his deliberate turning away from it, as like one who rose to the sky and then descended, as He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut, who bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. He counted them as having been brought out of the light, though they never entered it, but they were capable of it. In his explanation, there is a likening of the scattered thoughts of the unbeliever to the snatching birds, and in the likening of Satan's casting down to the wind carrying one into a remote place, there is scrutiny, because both matters were mentioned in the context of dividing the state of the unbeliever into two parts. If the first is made an example of the divergence of desires and thoughts, and the second an example of Satan's incitement, then he has made them one thing, because the scattering of thoughts and the divergence of desires are attributed to Satan's incitement, so the intended division is not realized. What appears in the explanation of the two likenesses is other than that. We say: when the state of disbelief was divided into two parts with no more beyond them, the first of them is the wavering one, persisting in doubt and not resolving upon a single error. This kind of polytheist is likened to one whom the birds have snatched and scattered, for no bird seizes a piece of him without another snatching it from it, and that is the state of the wavering one: no fancy appears to him without his following it and descending from what he was upon. The second is a polytheist resolved upon a false belief, who, even if sawn with a saw, would not yield or turn back; there is no way to make him doubt, and no hope of moving him from what he is upon, for he rejoices and is delighted in his error.

This one is likened, in his persistence in his disbelief, to the settling of one whom the wind has thrown into a low valley where he settles. The likeness to settling in the remote valley, which is the furthest of abysses from the sky, is evident. He described his error as distant in His saying: ﴿Those are in distant error﴾ [Ibrahim: 3] and ﴿They have certainly strayed far away﴾ [al-Nisa': 167], i.e., they resolved upon their error, so their return to the truth became remote. This is the realization of the two divisions, and Allah knows best. End of his words.

It is not hidden that in the noble text there is room for this, though there is no decisive proof for it. Yes, it is a marvelous deduction and a subtle extraction. May Allah have mercy on its copyist.

Ibn Kathir said: Allah, exalted is He, has struck for the polytheists another parable in Surat al-An'am, which is His saying: ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah what neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have led astray in the earth, bewildered, having companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us." Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 71], and so on.

(p-٤٣٤١) The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[32] ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah – indeed, it is from the piety of hearts.﴾

﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah﴾ – i.e., the signs of His guidance, which is the religion (al-din). Or the landmarks (ma'alim) of the Hajj and its rites (manasik). Or specifically the sacrificial animals (al-hada_ya), because they are among the landmarks and symbols of the Hajj of the Exalted, as the verse indicates: ﴿And the camels – We have made them for you among the symbols of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 36], and this is most fitting with what follows it. Honoring them is that one chooses them large in body, beautiful, fat, and high in price, and forgoes haggling (al-mikas) over their purchase. For they used to pay high prices in three cases and disliked haggling over them: the sacrificial offering (al-hady), the sacrificial animal (al-udhiyya), and the slave (al-raqaba).

And on the authority of Sahl: "We used to fatten the sacrificial animal in Madinah, and the Muslims used to fatten them." Narrated by al-Bukhari.

And on the authority of Anas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sacrificed two horned rams, white with black markings." Narrated by al-Bukhari.

And on the authority of al-Bara', traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Four [defects] are not permitted in sacrificial animals: the one-eyed whose blindness is evident, the sick whose sickness is evident, the lame whose limping is evident, and the emaciated that has no marrow." Narrated by Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan.

﴿Indeed, it﴾ – i.e., indeed, honoring them – ﴿is from the piety of hearts﴾ – i.e., it is among the acts of those who possess piety (taqwa). The attribution to the hearts is because piety and its opposite arise from them.

The Interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[33] ﴿For you there are benefits in them until an appointed term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House.﴾

﴿For you there are benefits in them until an appointed term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House.﴾ That is: for you in the sacrificial animals (al-hadaya) there are benefits, their milk, their offspring, their wool and their backs, until the time of their slaughter. It has been related in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn) from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw a man driving a camel for sacrifice (badana), and he said: 'Ride it.' The man said: 'It is a badana.' He said: 'Ride it, woe to you, [even] on the second or third [occasion].'"

His words ﴿then their place of sacrifice﴾ mean: the place where the sacrificial animals are slaughtered and where they end up is at the Ancient House, which is the Ka'bah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], and He said: ﴿and the offering held back from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25].

In (al-Iklil), it is said: "This indicates that the hadi (sacrificial animal) is not slaughtered except within the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram)." It was also said: the meaning is that the place of all these rites (sha'a'ir) is the circumambulation (tawaf) around the Ancient House. This implies that the pilgrim, after the tawaf al-ifadah, becomes permitted to do everything. Similarly it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas: "No one circumambulates the House except that he becomes permitted (halla), because of this verse." And His words, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He:

[34] ﴿And for every community We have appointed rites, that they may mention the name of Allah over the livestock He has provided for them. For your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble.﴾

﴿And for every community We have appointed rites, that they may mention the name of Allah over the livestock He has provided for them﴾ (p-٤٣٤٣) That is: We legislated for every community that they perform the rite of *nusk* (sacrifice). That is: they slaughter for His sake, exalted be He, seeking nearness to Him. He made the reason that His name be mentioned, may His names be sanctified, over the sacrificial animals (*nasa'ik*). So *manasik* is a *masdar mimi* (a verbal noun formed with the prefix *mim*) in its original form, or in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ul*). And in the verse there is an indication that the sacrifice (*qurban*) must be from livestock (*ni'am*).

﴿So your God is one God, so submit to Him﴾ That is: devote the remembrance (*dhikr*) to Him alone, and do not mix it with association (*shirk*). ﴿And give good tidings to the humble﴾

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[35–36] ﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and those who are patient over what befalls them, and those who establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them.﴾ ﴿And the camels We have made for you as among the symbols of Allah; in them is good for you. So mention the name of Allah over them as they stand in ranks. Then when they fall on their sides, eat from them and feed the contented and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you, so that you may be grateful.﴾ [al-Hajj: 36].

﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾: that is, they fear, because of their great impression when He is mentioned. ﴿And those who are patient over what befalls them, and those who establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them﴾. ﴿And the camels We have made for you as among the symbols of Allah; in them is good for you﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]: that is, in slaughtering them as a sacrifice. ﴿Good﴾ [al-Hajj: 36] from religious and worldly benefits. ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them as they stand in ranks﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]: that is, standing, having arranged their forelegs and hind legs. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "standing on three legs, its left foreleg tied, saying: In the name of Allah, Allah is greatest, there is no god but Allah; O Allah, from You and to You." In the two Sahihs, it is related from Ibn ʿUmar that he passed by a man who had made a camel kneel and was slaughtering it, and he said: "Send it up standing, tied, the sunnah of Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ)." In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, in the description of the Farewell Pilgrimage, he said in it: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slaughtered sixty-three camels with his own hand. He began stabbing them with a spear in his hand." ﴿Then when they fall on their sides﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]: that is, they fell to the ground, and this is a metaphor for death. ﴿Then eat from them and feed the contented﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]: that is, the one who asks. ﴿And the beggar﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]: that is, the one who presents himself without asking. Or, the contented is one who is satisfied with what he has and with what is given to him without asking, and the beggar is one who presents himself by asking. It has been deduced that the sacrificial animal is divided into three parts: he eats one third, gives one third as a gift, and gives one third in charity.

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you, so that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]: that is, We made them submissive to you, so that you may thank Our bounty. Gratitude is the servant's directing of what he has been blessed with toward that for which it was created.

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[37] ﴿It is not their meat that reaches God, nor their blood, but it is piety from you that reaches Him. Thus He subjected them to you so that you may magnify God for guiding you. And give good tidings to the doers of good.﴾

﴿It is not their meat that reaches God, nor their blood, but it is piety from you that reaches Him.﴾ That is: their meat, which is given in charity, does not attain His good pleasure, nor does their blood, which is shed, insofar as they are meat and blood. Rather, it is by observing the intention and sincerity, seeking His Most High Countenance. Close to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Righteousness is not that you turn your faces [toward the east and the west]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], to the end of it. ﴿Thus He subjected them to you so that you may magnify God for guiding you.﴾ That is: so that you may know His greatness and thereby single Him out in worship, for He has guided you to the way of making them subject to you and to the manner of drawing near to Him through them, upon the tongue of His most noble messenger, sent with the happiness of both abodes. He repeated it to remind of the blessing and as a reason for what follows. (p. 4345) In this stated reason there is evidence for what we presented earlier concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and mention the name of God on known days over what He has provided them of the livestock animals﴾ [al-Hajj: 28], so reflect. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾, that is: to those who are sincere in their deeds.

The discussion of the words of God, Exalted is He:

[38] ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed. Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾ is a new independent statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to settle the hearts of the believers, by making clear that Allah, Exalted is He, is their helper against their enemies, to the extent that they will not be able to prevent them from performing the Hajj, so that they may devote themselves to performing its rites. Thus said Abu al-Suʿud, and al-Razi preceded him to this. The better view is to say that it is a forerunner (ṭaliʿa) of what follows of the permission to fight (al-idhn bi-l-qital), heralding for the believers the utmost victory, protection, safeguarding and good outcome, as encouragement for them to fight those who wronged them, and as an incitement toward reclaiming His Sacred House, so that they may be able to establish its rites and perform its ceremonies. As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate﴾, meaning: in regard to the trust of Allah — ﴿ingrate﴾, meaning: toward His blessing by worshipping other than Him. So He does not approve of their deed, nor does He help them. The intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah) is used in both of these, because it concerns the polytheists, and they are such, and because betraying the trust of Allah and ingratitude for His blessing is not a trivial matter, but rather a grave one.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[39–40] ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And indeed, God is able to give them victory.﴾ ﴿They are those who have been driven from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is God." And had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, prayer-houses and mosques, in which the name of God is much mentioned, would surely have been demolished. God will surely help those who help Him. Indeed, God is Powerful, Mighty.﴾ [al-Hajj: 40].

﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against﴾, i.e., those who are fought by the polytheists. The object of the permission is omitted, because what is mentioned points to it. It was also read with a kasra on the tā' (يُقاتِلُونَ), meaning "those who fight." ﴿because they have been wronged. And indeed, God is able to give them victory.﴾ ﴿They are those who have been driven from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is God"﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], i.e., without any right other than monotheism, which should be the cause of acknowledgment and empowerment, not the cause of expulsion and exile. A similar verse is: ﴿Do you resent us for nothing except that we believed in God?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59], and this is an emphasis of praise expressed in a form that resembles blame.

﴿And had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, prayer-houses and mosques, in which the name of God is much mentioned, would surely have been demolished﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], i.e., had He not restrained the polytheists by means of the Muslims, and had He not permitted the Muslims to strive against the disbelievers, the polytheists would have overpowered the adherents of the various religions in their times, and demolished their places of worship.

Ibn Jarir said: Among this is His restraining some of them from wronging others, like a ruler by whom He restrains his subjects from wronging one another. Among it is also His restraining, through some of them, one who is permitted to give testimony among them from going off with the right of someone who has a claim against him, and the like. All of this is a repelling by Him of some people from others. Were it not for that, they would wrong one another. So the dominant would demolish the monasteries and churches of the subdued, and He, may His praise be glorified, did not name them.

The ṣawāmiʿ (صَوامِعُ, monasteries) are the buildings of monasticism, because of the seclusion of its people. The biyaʿ (بِيَعُ, churches) are the places of worship of the Christians. The ṣalawāt (صَلَواتُ, prayer-houses): it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he meant by them the synagogues of the Jews, and they were so named because they are the place of prayer. It was also said that they are in their literal meaning.

HudDimat (هُدِّمَتْ, "were demolished") is in the sense of "were rendered useless." Or there is an implied omitted noun in it.

﴿God will surely help those who help Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], i.e., will help His religion and His allies.

Al-Qadi said: God has fulfilled His promise, by empowering the Emigrants and the Helpers over the chiefs of the Arabs and the kings of the Persians and the Caesars of them, and made them inherit their land and their homes. ﴿Indeed, God is Powerful, Mighty.﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]

Al-Qadi said: God has fulfilled His promise, by empowering the Emigrants and the Helpers over the chiefs of the Arabs and the kings of the Persians and the Caesars of them, and made them inherit their land and their homes. ﴿Indeed, God is Powerful, Mighty.﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]

The discussion of the interpretation (*ta'wil*, explanation) of His saying:

[41] ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And with Allah is the outcome of affairs.﴾

(p. 4347) ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And with Allah is the outcome of affairs.﴾ That is: its return is to His judgment and His decree. In it is an affirmation of what He promised regarding the manifestation of His allies and the elevation of their word. Then Exalted is He pointed to consoling His Prophet (ﷺ) for the harm he suffers from the polytheists, and urging him to be patient over the denial he meets from them, by His saying, glorified is He:

**The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[42–44] ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Thamud had denied before them﴾ ﴿and the people of Abraham, and the people of Lot﴾ [al-Hajj: 43] ﴿and the companions of Madyan. And Moses was denied. So I gave the disbelievers respite, then I seized them; so how was My disapproval?﴾ [al-Hajj: 44].

﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah, and 'Ad﴾: and they are the people of Hud. ﴿And Thamud﴾: and they are the people of Salih. ﴿And the people of Abraham, and the people of Lot﴾ [al-Hajj: 43]. ﴿And the companions of Madyan﴾ [al-Hajj: 44]: and they are the people of Shu'ayb. ﴿And Moses was denied﴾ [al-Hajj: 44]. He did not say "the people of Moses" as He did with the previous ones, because Moses was not denied by his own people, the Children of Israel. Rather, he was denied by others than his people, namely the Qibt (Copts).

There is also another point in this: it is as if it was said, after mentioning the denial of every people of their messenger: ﴿And Moses was denied﴾ [al-Hajj: 44] despite the clarity of his signs and the greatness of his miracles, so what do you think about others? This was conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Nasir said: "It is possible in my view, and God knows best, that when He opened the discourse with the narration of their denial, and then enumerated the categories of the deniers and their groups, and had not reached Moses except after a long discourse, it was good to repeat it so that it would come directly before His saying: ﴿So I gave the disbelievers respite﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], so that the consequence would be connected to the cause. Just as He said in the verse of Qaf, after enumerating them: ﴿Each denied the messengers, so My warning was justified﴾ [Qaf: 14], linking the punishment and the warning and joining them to the chastisement, after He had renewed the mention of it. And God knows best."

As for the objection of one who claims that Moses was denied by his people through the worship of the calf, this is the objection of one who did not understand the meaning of denial, which is rejecting the call of the Prophet, not believing in him, persisting in disbelief in his revelation, standing against him, and preventing people from following him. What happened from the people of Moses was confusion, an error of ijtihad (independent reasoning), obstinacy and stubbornness, while sheltering under the shade of his call and joining the ranks of those who answered him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I gave the disbelievers respite﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], meaning: I gave them time. ﴿Then I seized them﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], meaning: with punishment. ﴿So how was My disapproval?﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], meaning: My rejection of them through destruction.
